title: TCP vs UDP: The Cost of Reliability

sources.title: RFC 9293 — Transmission Control Protocol
sources.notes: Byte-stream service, sequence numbers, SYN/FIN sequence space, three-way handshake, cumulative acknowledgments and receive windows.

sources.title: RFC 768 — User Datagram Protocol
sources.notes: UDP datagram service does not guarantee delivery or duplicate protection.

sources.title: RFC 5681 — TCP Congestion Control
sources.notes: Congestion window and receiver window are distinct constraints on sending.

sources.title: RFC 9000 — QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport
sources.notes: QUIC demonstrates reliable transport capabilities layered over UDP datagrams.

sections.title: Two transports, one unreliable network
sections.narration: Both transports cross a network that can lose or reorder traffic. Watch different responses to failure. The useful choice concerns application behavior, not a universal fast-versus-slow label.
bullets: IP can lose or reorder packets
sections.takeaway: Choose a transport by the behavior the application needs.

sections.title: Ports identify application endpoints
sections.narration: An IP address identifies a network endpoint. Ports distinguish transport endpoints there. Follow a destination-port field toward the matching application, rather than treating ports as physical sockets.
sections.takeaway: Ports help a host deliver incoming transport data to the right endpoint.

sections.title: UDP preserves datagram boundaries
sections.narration: UDP sends distinct datagrams. If one arrives intact, its boundary remains meaningful to the receiving application. UDP itself does not promise delivery, ordering, or suppression of duplicate datagrams.
bullets: No built-in delivery or order guarantee
sections.takeaway: UDP exposes datagrams without TCP’s reliable ordered byte-stream service.

sections.title: TCP exposes a byte stream
sections.narration: TCP presents ordered bytes rather than the original application write boundaries. Watch HEL, LO, and an exclamation mark become one stream. Applications must supply their own message framing.
sections.takeaway: TCP preserves byte order, not the application’s original write boundaries.

sections.title: First establish a connection
sections.narration: Before this TCP exchange, the endpoints synchronize sequence information through a three-way handshake. Follow the state changes as the control messages travel, rather than imagining a reserved physical circuit.
sections.takeaway: The handshake synchronizes both directions of sequence space.

sections.title: Step one: the client sends SYN
sections.narration: Our client starts with sequence number one hundred. Its SYN consumes one sequence position, so its first data byte will be numbered one hundred and one in this example.
bullets: First client data will start at 101
sections.takeaway: SYN consumes one sequence number.

sections.title: Step two: SYN plus acknowledgment
sections.narration: The server chooses initial sequence five hundred and acknowledges one hundred and one. The acknowledgment refers to the client's sequence space; the server's SYN starts its own independent space.
bullets: Each direction has its own numbering
sections.takeaway: An acknowledgment names the next sequence position expected.

sections.title: Step three: acknowledge the server
sections.narration: The client acknowledges five hundred and one and can use sequence one hundred and one for its next data. Both directions now have synchronized state for this established connection.
bullets: ACK alone consumes no sequence number
sections.takeaway: Both endpoints now know the peer’s starting sequence space.

sections.title: Number bytes, not whole packets
sections.narration: Send one hundred bytes beginning at sequence one hundred and one. Their numbers run through two hundred. TCP sequence numbers count stream positions, not the number of visible packets.
sections.takeaway: A segment’s sequence number identifies its first data byte.

sections.title: Cumulative acknowledgment
sections.narration: ACK two hundred and one confirms all preceding data in this example. It names the next byte expected. The acknowledged prefix matters more than how those bytes were packetized.
sections.takeaway: TCP’s acknowledgment number identifies the next expected byte.

sections.title: Packets arrive out of order
sections.narration: Bytes three hundred and one through four hundred arrive while two hundred and one through three hundred are missing. They can wait in reassembly storage; the cumulative acknowledgment stays two hundred and one.
bullets: Later bytes can wait in a buffer
sections.takeaway: Receiving later data does not remove an earlier gap in an ordered stream.

sections.title: Recover the missing byte range
sections.narration: Retransmit the missing middle range. Once it arrives, the contiguous prefix reaches four hundred, and ACK four hundred and one can advance. Ordered application delivery can now continue.
sections.takeaway: Reliability comes from detecting gaps and retransmitting missing data.

sections.title: A lost acknowledgment is not lost data
sections.narration: The receiver got bytes one hundred and one through two hundred, but its ACK disappears. A repeated segment must not become duplicate stream delivery. The receiver can acknowledge the confirmed prefix again.
bullets: Duplicate bytes are not delivered twice
sections.takeaway: Sequence space supports duplicate detection as well as ordering.

sections.title: Reliability adds state and delay
sections.narration: Later bytes may be buffered while a missing range blocks ordered stream delivery. Reliability therefore requires storage and recovery time. Watch the gap hold up data the application cannot yet consume.
bullets: An early gap can delay later bytes
sections.takeaway: Reliability is a useful service with resource and timing costs.

sections.title: Protect the receiver with flow control
sections.narration: The receiver advertises available receive space. Two hundred arriving bytes occupy part of our three-hundred-byte buffer, leaving one hundred. Flow control prevents overwhelming this receiving endpoint's available storage.
sections.takeaway: Flow control addresses the receiver’s capacity.

sections.title: Watch the receive window change
sections.narration: Fill the remaining hundred bytes: advertised space reaches zero. Then let the application consume two hundred bytes. The freed capacity can be advertised, permitting sending to continue appropriately.
sections.takeaway: An advertised window can change as the application drains its buffer.

sections.title: Congestion control protects the path
sections.narration: The receiver can have room while a router's queue is full. Congestion control responds to path conditions, separately from receiver flow control. Effective sending must respect both constraints.
bullets: Receiver capacity differs from path load
sections.takeaway: Flow control protects the receiver; congestion control protects the network.

sections.title: UDP under the same packet loss
sections.narration: Under UDP alone, the missing second datagram is not automatically retransmitted. Later datagrams can still arrive. The application must decide whether recovery, replacement, or accepting the gap fits its purpose.
bullets: Missing datagrams stay missing in UDP
The application decides how to react
sections.takeaway: UDP does not add TCP’s retransmission and ordering behavior.

sections.title: Applications can build above UDP
sections.narration: An application protocol can add acknowledgments, retransmission, encryption, and congestion control above UDP. UDP's minimal service does not forbid reliability; those features simply come from another layer.
bullets: QUIC adds a richer transport service
sections.takeaway: A UDP-based protocol can implement capabilities absent from UDP itself.

sections.title: Faster is the wrong universal label
sections.narration: UDP omits TCP's particular connection and reliability machinery, but experienced delay depends on application design and network conditions. Watch failure and recovery costs instead of assigning one permanent speed winner.
bullets: Less built-in machinery is not a guarantee
sections.takeaway: Transport choice does not create a universal speed ranking.

sections.title: Choose a service for a file transfer
sections.narration: A file transfer normally needs all its bytes in order. Filling the gap allows complete reconstruction. TCP provides a suitable stream service, while the application still handles framing and failures.
bullets: Security and durable storage are separate
sections.takeaway: TCP reliability is transport delivery, not every application guarantee.

sections.title: Choose a service for timely updates
sections.narration: For some position updates, a newer state can replace an old missing one. Watch the display accept later information. That policy belongs to the application, not a general UDP guarantee.
bullets: Fresh updates may replace stale ones
sections.takeaway: A useful transport matches the meaning and timing of application data.
sections.short_title: Prefer a fresh update when appropriate

sections.title: Connections also need an ending
sections.narration: TCP can close its two directions separately. FIN consumes a sequence position, and acknowledgments confirm it. Follow the example numbers without assuming every close follows one identical timing pattern.
sections.takeaway: Connection release is part of the transport’s state machine.

sections.title: Answer the transport puzzle
sections.narration: TCP supplies a reliable ordered byte stream; UDP exposes datagrams without those built-in guarantees. Choose according to completeness, ordering, timeliness, and the behavior your application will add itself.
sections.takeaway: Understand the service contract before choosing the transport.
